production-regions-s1.title: What three kinds of farming can pay for land

plot.label: Line chart of the rent three kinds of farming can pay per hectare at distances from 0 to 100 km from a market: market gardening starts highest and falls fastest, reaching zero at 45 km; grain starts lower and falls more slowly, reaching zero at about 67 km; ranching starts lowest and falls slowest, reaching zero at 100 km.
plot.yLabel: Rent a farmer can pay (dollars per hectare)

production-regions-s2.title: Farm output sold for cash, by province of Country A

map.label: Choropleth of Country A by province: the share of farm output that is sold is highest in the Capital Region and Central Valley and lowest in the Southern Forest and Northern Hills
map.legendTitle: Farm output sold for cash (percent, invented)

items.q: According to the chart, which kind of farming can pay the highest rent for land 10 km from the market?
options: Market gardening
Grain
Ranching
The three can pay about the same

why.correct: Read up from 10 km on the distance axis: the market gardening line is highest, so that use would outbid the others for this land.
options: Right: at 10 km market gardening can pay about 700 dollars a hectare, more than grain or ranching.
Grain can pay about 340 dollars a hectare at 10 km, less than market gardening.
Ranching can pay the least near the market, about 140 dollars a hectare.
The lines are far apart at 10 km.

items.q: Between 40 and 50 km from the market, which kind of farming can pay the most for land?
options: Market gardening
Ranching
Grain
Ranching and grain equally

why.correct: Bid-rent theory says land goes to the use that can pay the most. In the middle band that is grain, so a ring of grain farms forms there.
options: Market gardening falls fast and reaches zero at 45 km.
Ranching overtakes grain past about 56 km, beyond this band.
Right: past about 36 km the grain line is above the market gardening line, and it stays above ranching until about 56 km.
Grain is well above ranching between 40 and 50 km; they cross only past about 56 km.

items.q: Why does the market gardening line fall faster than the ranching line?
options: Ranchers sell their animals at a much higher price per hectare
Vegetables grow faster far away from the market
Market gardens need less labor for each hectare
Its fresh produce costs more to ship and spoils on long trips

why.correct: The slope shows how fast transport costs eat into what a use can earn. Perishable produce has the steepest slope.
options: Ranching earns little per hectare; that is why its line starts lowest.
Growth rate does not change with distance; shipping cost and spoilage do.
Market gardens need much more labor per hectare, not less.
Right: perishable, bulky produce loses value fast with distance, so the rent it can pay drops quickly.

items.q: A new highway and refrigerated trucks cut the cost of shipping fresh produce. How would the market gardening line most likely change?
options: It would fall more steeply, so gardening would move closer in to town
It would fall less steeply, so gardening could extend farther out
It would match the ranching line exactly
It would disappear from the chart

why.correct: Transport technology changes bid-rent patterns: when distance costs less, intensive uses can spread farther from the market.
options: Cheaper shipping lowers the cost of distance, which flattens the line.
Right: lower transport cost flattens the line, so market gardening can outbid grain over a wider area.
Cheaper shipping helps produce most, so its line does not drop to ranching's.
Market gardening remains profitable near the market.

items.q: Which statement describes the pattern on the map?
options: Sold output is highest in the Southern Forest and lowest near the capital
Sold output is about equal across the provinces of the country
Sold output peaks near the capital and is lowest in the far south and north
Sold output is highest along the South Coast and lowest in the Central Valley

why.correct: A pattern names where values are high and low: highest around the capital and Central Valley, lowest in the forest and hills at the edges.
options: The legend shows the reverse: the Southern Forest is in the lowest class.
The provinces fall into four different classes.
Right: the darkest class is in the Capital Region and Central Valley; the lightest is in the Southern Forest and Northern Hills.
The Central Valley is in the highest class.

items.q: What is the scale of analysis of the data on this map?
options: Local (subnational): each value is for a province
National: the map shows the whole country
Global: the data compare countries of the world
Regional: the data compare world regions

why.correct: The scale of analysis is the scale of the data shown, not the size of the area drawn. Province data are local (subnational).
options: Right: the data describe parts of one country, so they are subnational.
The scale of analysis is the scale of the data. Each value is for a province, not for the country.
Only one country is shown.
The values are for provinces of one country.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the low share of sold output in the Southern Forest?
options: Land near the capital is cheap, so farmers there grow food to eat
Far from the capital's market, more families grow food to eat
Forest provinces have the highest rents in the country
Farmers in the forest sell most of their crops abroad

why.correct: Bid-rent and access go together: near the main market, land is costly and farms sell most of what they grow; far away, more farming is for the family's own use.
options: Land near a large market usually costs more, pushing farmers to grow for sale.
Right: where markets are distant and transport is costly, subsistence agriculture is more common.
Rents are usually lowest far from the main market.
The map shows that most output there is not sold.
Farming mainly to sell crops for profit
Growing one crop on the same field year after year
Raising animals on fixed, fenced grassland
Farming mainly to feed the farmer's own family

why.correct: Subsistence agriculture grows food for the farming household; commercial agriculture grows it for sale.
options: That is commercial agriculture.
That is monocropping.
That is ranching, which is usually commercial.
Right: subsistence farmers eat most of what they grow and sell little.

items.q: A family in rural Bangladesh grows rice on a small plot and eats most of it, while a farm in Iowa sells all of its corn to a grain company. Which comparison is accurate?
options: The Bangladesh farm is subsistence, whereas the Iowa farm is commercial
Both farms are commercial, but Iowa's is larger
The Bangladesh farm is commercial, whereas the Iowa farm is subsistence
Both are subsistence farms because both grow grain

why.correct: A compare speaks of both sides: subsistence in Bangladesh, whereas commercial in Iowa.
options: Right: one grows mainly to eat, the other entirely to sell.
The Bangladesh family eats most of its crop, so it is not mainly commercial.
The labels are reversed.
What decides it is whether the crop is eaten or sold, not which crop it is.

items.q: In Mato Grosso, Brazil, huge farms grow soybeans across thousands of hectares. What is one risk of this monocropping?
options: The farm is too small to sell its crop to buyers
The farm grows too many different crops to manage
A pest or price drop can hit the whole harvest at once
The farm moves to a new forest plot after a few years

why.correct: Monocropping is efficient for machines and sales, but it puts all the risk on one crop and can wear down soils without rotation.
options: These farms are among the largest in the world and sell nearly all they grow.
Monocropping is the opposite: one crop.
Right: with one crop, a disease, pest or fall in price affects everything the farm grows.
That describes shifting cultivation, not large commercial soy farms.

items.q: According to bid-rent theory, why is land near a large market usually farmed intensively?
options: It costs less, so farmers can leave much of it unused for years
Its soil is the richest in the region
Farmers near markets are not allowed to keep animals
It costs more, so just high-earning uses can afford it

why.correct: Bid-rent theory: the closer to the market, the more land costs, and the more each hectare must earn. That favors intensive uses such as market gardening and dairy.
options: Land near a market costs more, not less.
Bid-rent theory explains land use by access and cost, not soil.
Bid-rent theory is about what users can pay, not about rules on animals.
Right: land users bid for access to the market; intensive uses earn enough per hectare to pay the high rent.

items.q: A market gardener earns 900 dollars a hectare at the market. Shipping costs 30 dollars a hectare for each km of distance. Using this simple bid-rent rule, what rent can the gardener pay for land 20 km away, in dollars per hectare?

mistakes.why: You subtracted the cost of 1 km only. Multiply the cost per km by the distance (30 × 20 = 600), then subtract.
600 is the shipping cost. Subtract it from the 900 the gardener earns at the market.

items.q: Build the bid-rent pattern: place each land use in the ring where it can pay the most, from the market outward.

model.title: Highest bidder at each distance from a market

slips.why: Ranching earns the least per hectare, so it cannot pay the high rent near the market; it ends up farthest out.
Bid-rent ranks commercial uses competing for land near one market; shifting cultivation is not one of them here.

why.correct: The use that earns most per hectare but loses value fastest with distance takes the center; uses with low earnings and cheap transport take the outer rings.

items.q: Rank the land uses by the rent each can pay right at the market, highest at the top.

model.title: Rent each use can pay at the market

slips.why: Grain earns less per hectare than fresh produce, so it cannot outbid market gardening at the market.

why.correct: At the market, intensive uses that earn much per hectare can pay the most rent: market gardening, then grain, then ranching.

items.q: Build a statement of one limit of bid-rent theory, applied to a real place.

why.correct: A model's limit names the assumption and a real place where it does not hold.

specific.model: Bid-rent theory assumes one market with equal transport in every direction, but in the Netherlands highways, rivers and several large cities give many places good access to markets.

limit.label: Assumption
options: one market with equal transport in every direction
farmers grow food mainly for their own families

why.1: Bid-rent theory is about commercial uses bidding for market access, not subsistence.

place.label: Place
options: the Netherlands
the Amazon rainforest

why.1: Pick a place with several markets and transport routes to show the limit.

effect.label: Why it fails there
options: highways, rivers and several large cities give many places good access to markets
all land is the same distance from the sea

why.1: Distance to the sea is not the point; many markets and routes break the single-center pattern.
